result.summary: Apollodorus follows Dionysus as he spreads his worship and punishes those who refuse him, then turns to the Theban royal house: Cadmus's end, the rise of Amphion and Zethus, Niobe's pride, and the story of Laius and Oedipus, who solves the Sphinx's riddle and ends in exile.

scenes.title: Dionysus and Lycurgus
scenes.summary: Mad Dionysus wanders to Phrygia, is initiated by Rhea, and is driven out by Lycurgus. Dionysus drives Lycurgus mad and he kills his son; the Edonians then put him to death.
scenes.stakes: Lycurgus risks the god's wrath for rejecting him; Dionysus risks his mission and his followers.

scenes.title: Dionysus at Thebes, Argos, sea
scenes.summary: Dionysus makes the Theban women rave, and Pentheus is torn apart by Agave. He drives the Argive women mad, turns pirates into dolphins, and brings his mother to heaven.
scenes.stakes: Pentheus and the pirates risk destruction for defying a god.

scenes.title: Cadmus and Harmonia leave
scenes.summary: Cadmus and Harmonia lead the Encheleans to victory over the Illyrians. They are turned into serpents and sent to the Elysian Fields.

scenes.title: Antiope and the twins
scenes.summary: Lycus usurps Thebes; Antiope's sons Zethus and Amphion kill Lycus, bind Dirce to a bull, fortify Thebes and expel Laius.
scenes.stakes: Antiope suffers captivity; Lycus and Dirce face vengeance.

scenes.title: Niobe's boast
scenes.summary: Niobe boasts she has more children than Latona. Artemis and Apollo kill the children, and Niobe turns to stone at Sipylus.
scenes.stakes: Niobe's children and her own life.

scenes.title: Laius, Oedipus and the crossroads
scenes.summary: Laius ignores the oracle and exposes his infant son, who is raised in Corinth as Oedipus. Warned at Delphi, he kills Laius on the road.
scenes.stakes: Oedipus is fated to kill his father and marry his mother.

scenes.title: The Sphinx and Oedipus's fall
scenes.summary: Oedipus solves the Sphinx's riddle, becomes king and marries Jocasta. When the truth emerges, she hangs herself and he blinds himself and goes into exile, dying at Colonus.
scenes.stakes: Thebes is losing its people to the Sphinx; Oedipus risks the fate foretold.

notable_quotes.reason: The Sphinx's famous riddle about the stages of human life.
The Delphic oracle's prophecy that drives Oedipus's tragedy.

analysis.text: Denying a god's power brings ruin, as Lycurgus, Pentheus and Niobe all find. Fate also works through attempts to avoid it, as with Laius and Oedipus.
Apollodorus gathers rival versions, such as Hesiod's and Homer's counts of Niobe's children, showing a mythographer's concern for variants.

legacy.text: The Oedipus story shaped Sophocles' tragedies and Freud's 'Oedipus complex'.
Euripides' The Bacchae dramatizes the death of Pentheus.

fun_facts.text: Oedipus means 'swollen foot', which Apollodorus explains from the pierced ankles.

language_notes.text: Rhea, mother of the gods, here purifies Dionysus of his madness; the 'costume' is the Bacchic dress he later wears when leading his followers.
Bacchanals are the followers of Dionysus (Bacchus), mainly women who worship him in ecstatic rites; Satyrs are woodland creatures in his train.
'Extremities' means hands and feet; the king mutilated his son's body, mistaking him for vine-wood.
'Declared oracularly' means the god announced it through an oracle, a divine pronouncement.
The pillars set up in India recall boundary markers erected by conquerors such as Heracles, marking the limit of Dionysus' travels.
'Howbeit' is archaic for 'however' or 'nevertheless'.
Dionysus' mother is Semele, killed by Zeus' lightning; he fetched her from Hades and renamed her Thyone, making her immortal.
The Encheleans ("eel-men") were a people of the region of Illyria, north-west of Greece, where Cadmus was said to have gone after leaving Thebes.
"The god" is left unnamed; it refers to the oracular god, usually Apollo, who speaks through an oracle.
The Elysian Fields were the blessed afterlife abode of favored heroes; Cadmus's transformation into a serpent is told in other versions as well.
"Like-minded with him" means Labdacus shared Pentheus's attitude of hostility to Dionysus, hence his ruin.
"Usurped" means seized power without right; Lycus acted as regent but took the throne for himself.
"Compassed the supreme power" means he obtained or gained full rule.
A neatherd is a cowherd, a herdsman who tends cattle.
"Treated her despitefully" means treated her with cruelty and contempt.
Amphion's lyre was so magical that stones moved of their own accord into place to form the walls of Thebes.
Hesiod, Herodorus and Homer are cited as ancient authorities who gave different numbers of Niobe's children, showing that the myth had varying versions.
"Incited" means urged or stirred them to take action against Niobe's children.
Telesilla was a Greek poet of Argos whose version of the story differs from the main account, here saving different children.
"Expose" means to abandon a newborn outdoors to die, a practice known in the ancient Greek world.
"Neatherds" are cattle herdsmen.
The name Oedipus is commonly explained as meaning "swollen foot", from the injury to his ankles.
"Supposititious" means falsely substituted; they taunted him that he was not the true son of his parents.
The riddle's answer is 'man': the voice is the same throughout life, while the number of feet changes.
'Read her riddle' means interpret or solve it; 'gobble him up' is a blunt, colloquial rendering of the Sphinx's devouring.
'Unwittingly' means without knowing; Oedipus did not know Jocasta was his mother. 'Begat' is archaic for 'fathered'.
A 'suppliant' is one who seeks protection at a sacred place, which made harming him an offence against the gods.

context_notes.text: Hera hated Dionysus as the son of Zeus and Semele, so she afflicted him with madness.
The Edonians were a Thracian people living near the Strymon river, in northern Greece.
Pentheus' death is the subject of Euripides' play The Bacchae; Cithaeron is a mountain near Thebes.
Tyrrhenians were often portrayed in Greek myth as pirates.
Zeus (Greek god, king of the gods) frequently fathered heroes by mortal women; Antiope's twins are his sons.
Dirce's punishment, being dragged by a bull, was repaid for her cruelty to Antiope; the spring at Thebes bore her name.
Laius later became father of Oedipus; his abduction of Chrysippus was traditionally seen as bringing a curse on his house.
Latona (Leto) had only two children, Apollo and Artemis, so Niobe's boast was an insult to the goddess.
Sipylus is a mountain in Lydia, Asia Minor; a weeping rock there was identified with Niobe.
Delphi was the site of Apollo's oracle, where the Pythia gave prophecies consulted across Greece.
Phocis is the region of central Greece containing Delphi; the narrow road where the two met is the famous crossroads.
Hera is the queen of the gods. The Sphinx was a monster with a woman's face and a lion's body, sent to plague Thebes.
The Eumenides, 'the kindly ones', are the Furies under a softened name. Theseus was the legendary king of Athens.

literary_notes.text: Lycurgus destroys his son while thinking he is pruning the vine he scorned, a cruel reversal of his hatred of Dionysus' gift.
Pentheus goes to spy on the rites and is killed by his own mother, who mistakes him for an animal.
The pirates' transformation into dolphins gives their punishment a fitting form: they leap into the sea and become its creatures.
Bonds loosing "of themselves" implies unseen divine help, rescuing Antiope and setting up the sons' revenge.
Dirce suffers the same cruelty she inflicted on Antiope, giving the story a sense of fitting retribution.
Niobe's transformation into weeping stone turns her endless grief into a lasting image.
The oracle's warning about the son killing his father sets up the later murder, and Laius's drunken disobedience starts the tragedy.
Oedipus, fleeing his prophecy, fulfills it by killing Laius, his real father, on the road.
Calling a staff a 'third support' treats it as a foot, which resolves the riddle's image of a creature with three feet.
The reader knows the woman is Oedipus's mother while he does not, so his reward is already tragic.
The man who solved the riddle of humanity is ruined by ignorance of his own identity, and his sons offer him no help.
